commentary: Assess the effectiveness of the options available to organic and biodynamic grape growers to control pests and diseases. This question was answered by only one third of the candidates, and overall, not very successfully. Most did not define 'effectiveness', particularly the economic/financial implications. Nor were there many papers that clearly understood the conceptual differences between organic and biodynamic options (containment vs. prevention). Some papers treated some means of control as uniquely organic, such as pheromone usage and raptor control, when in fact these are now standard practices under sustainable and even many conventional growing systems. In too many instances, examples did not distinguish between organic and biodynamic. While many papers successfully discussed pest and disease control treatments using copper or sulphur, and habitat for predator animals, too few dealt with control through canopy management. Far too many papers described, but did not assess the options as the paper requires. Quoting one Examiner: "This essay reads like a list of pests/diseases and measures growers use to address them." The question required the use of analytical skills to address fundamental decisions vital to grape growers with more limited resources relative to conventional growers. 2.

commentary: What practical options does a viticulturist have at his or her disposal to address long term changes in climate in an established vineyard? A paper answered by over half the candidates, generally successfully. Absolutely critical to success here was defining 'Long Term' and also noting the answer had to be about an established vineyard. Some form of temporal notation (25-50 years, 40-75 years), with ensuing logical consideration and concrete examples, was also necessary. Many papers simply mentioned various, current vineyard 5 issues (such as faster ripening, more drought and extreme weather issues like hail) without putting their discussion into the long-term perspective. Although a majority of papers did cover issues relating to heat, drought and canopy, few grasped that long term solutions might need to include style change. For example vines might need to be top grafted over to a more appropriate variety or clone. And although canopy management changes were considered important over the long term, few papers considered below ground management techniques to improve water retention. Good candidates often pointed out the long term option of the abandonment of legal restrictions on irrigation in European countries. The best papers considered not just the global warming aspects of long term climate change, but the opposite issues in some areas such as increased and more dramatic frost events, more powerful rainstorms and the pros and cons of hail netting, factoring in both practical and the regulatory aspects. 3.

commentary: Can Cabernet Sauvignon and Riesling be successful in the same location? While a good percentage of candidates attempted this question, few succeeded with a convincing response. Three key issues needed consideration: 1) A brief review of the requirements for both varieties; 2) definition of 'successful'; 3) definition of 'same location'. Candidates then had to take a position. A few papers misinterpreted the question to mean 'high quality' wines only. Examiners caution candidates not to read too much into a question. Given the defined scope of this question, good answers were expected to show appropriate detail of where, why, and when these two varieties can co-exist successfully. Too many papers indicated broad locations, such as Napa or Austria. Good papers more correctly cited 'meso-areas', for example Clare Valley, or Columbia Valley/Yakima Valley. A couple of insightful papers suggested Germany's Pfalz, (even though little cabernet is there, it is warm enough to ripen marginally), and Alto Adige Italy. Not enough papers considered such currently successful 'same locations' as Canada's Okanagan Valley, the Margaret River or Great Southern appellations, Oregon's Umpqua Valley or less well known but plausible locations such as Israel's Northern Galilee hills. Far too many answers showed genuine ignorance of the climatic requirements for these varieties. Good answers did note that high quality viticultural practices yield positive results even when the climate conditions are challenging, while poor papers failed to discuss the viticultural factors that can allow success for both varieties in the same location. Good candidates also acknowledged that both varieties adapt easily to different conditions, both have hard wood for overwintering, and are relatively easy to grow in many different soils and climates. 4.

The question says "compare"- a mere description of each region's system(s) was not sufficient. It was important (and necessary for a Pass) to consider all four areas. Candidates 6 needed to think like a viticulturist/producer to know why certain systems are used in respective locations, and why others would or would not be effective. The best papers looked at how the respective systems fit into the local concept of terroir, and how they effectively dealt with the various issues of water availability, exposure, ideal varietal cropping levels, vine vigor manifestation, insolation and other factors. As an example, a couple of papers explained why the Mosel Arch system is used (steep slopes, near impossibility of using wired rows, better fruit insolation). Good papers also compared where the same systems (VSP in Mosel, Alsace) were practiced but for different situations or purposes. Some also considered how, for example in Alsace, both variety and terrain dictated different systems of VSP; cane vs arched cane, vs cordon, and differing strategies for leaf removal, pruning, air circulation and fungal prevention. The best candidates also recognised that in some areas, particularly Châteauneuf du Pape, different systems may be used for different varieties. Many simply put down bush vines/gobelet, forgetting that for Syrah guyot on wire is preferred. The nature of this question demanded concrete examples. Papers that provided 'textbook' examples sometimes reflected inexperience or lack of knowledge. 5.

The best responses for this question were awarded some of the highest marks for all of Paper 1, reflecting confident understanding and excellent knowledge of the subject. 6.

Attempted by a good number of candidates and showing strong marks, this was a highly topical question, in the light of the previous spring's events in several regions. Good answers realised and responded to the four parts of the question: WHEN / HOW / PREVENTION / RESPONSE. Examples 7 had to be global in nature and needed to discuss the weather conditions that lead to hailstorms, when they happen, how that timing dictates type and severity of damage and how to prevent or respond appropriately. A long detailed discussion of the 'cause' of hail was unnecessary, but it was important to consider the basic mechanism and, more importantly, at what periods/conditions it becomes a serious issue, followed by an assessment of potential means of prevention or response to damage. Less successful papers omitted one or more aspects of the question. Some answered well the 'when and how', but little on response, and no mention of treatments such as re-pruning. The best papers detailed certain less obvious and immediate problems, such as strong spring hail stripping new buds and destroying the coming vintage, with quantitative repercussions for up to two years. To most candidates' credit there was good knowledge of what kind of damage occurs at specific times, though not always as clear an understanding of what to do as a result. There was plenty of discussion, not always accurate, about the methods and efficacy of such treatments such as cloud seeding, anti hail cannons or netting. Good papers did note the legal restrictions in some places for these treatments, also commenting that the rationale for these restrictions may be flawed, though more study is needed. 8

commentary: It is often noted that some wines are not perfectly clean, and have low levels of potentially faulty aromas, sometimes referred to as "funky". How can a winemaker best manage a desirable element of "funkiness" in his or her wine?  Key Understanding: - The candidate needs to present a balanced view of the sometimes opposing notions on ideas concerning wine hygiene and demonstrate the difference between a fault and a desirable/complexing character intended to be part of the style. Controlled "funkiness" is a very different thing to random spoilage from poor winemaking practices. Candidates will need to put together a convincing argument as to what "funky" wines entail. This will require some explanation of what potentially faulty/funky aromas consist and secondly how one can best manage them. It is important that the candidates show breadth and depth of knowledge across all premium quality wine styles globally including sparkling and fortified wines. Candidates should not just discuss 'natural' wines. A question that required a tight definition of 'funk' and some good practical examples, plus an understanding of the key words 'manage' and 'desirable'. Unfortunately, a very low pass mark resulted because candidates failed in these areas. This was a topical question that should have offered plenty of opportunities for candidates to discuss one of the more interesting and controversial areas of winemaking. Passing answers were able to firstly define funkiness clearly (ideally as something belonging to the grey area between fault and complexity), clearly point to key characteristics within the winemaker's control that fall into these grey areas (4-EP/4-EG, both reduction and oxidation characters, extended skin contact, etc), and then outline some winemaking steps that would permit the winemaker to end up with a desirable amount/element. Disappointingly, far too many answers had weak, poor or no definitions of 'funk', instead subverting the question to a discussion of faults. While almost all candidates were able to identify the key 9 purveyors of 'funk' in wine, there were several that simply focused on one (usually Brett) or missed important ones. A number of other candidates were insufficiently armed with accurate technical knowledge. Almost without exception answers that failed did so for failing to answer the question. Many simply dropped a detailed list of the characteristics of Brett, oxidation or reduction, quite a number lacked accurate technical knowledge, while most simply pointed to steps to eliminate rather than manage a desirable element of Brett, oxidation, reduction etc. The predictable examples of Musar, Beaucastel, Grange etc continue to appear but these are now decades old - there is a whole world of modern winemaking examples to draw on that would make candidates' papers more distinctive and original. Overall, the Examiners commented that candidates are focussing on gathering a lot of examples and using them as a substitute for critical thinking. Some papers give a number of examples as facts, with little or no context, critical assessment and rarely a counter-example to drive home a point. Examples are well used when they support a persuasive argument, not act as substitute for one. 2.

commentary: How can a wine's tannin profile be managed during vinification? Key understanding: The question clearly states "during vinification" so candidates should limit themselves to the winemaking process. A brief mention of harvesting grapes at optimum phenolic ripeness is fine but candidates must focus on the winemaking. Candidates must demonstrate an understanding of the tannin extraction processes, the use of aids to extract, add and / or fix tannins and the use of oak tannins. Candidates could also discuss microoxygenation. Mention could be made of white, sparkling, sweet and fortified wine but should focus on red winemaking. This question had the highest pass rate in the Paper. The less successful scripts tended to either offer 'all I know about tannin', in rather chatty style, or provided a lot of technical detail about the subject but were unable to interpret that detail into a sensible argument. With these types of questions a logical flow to the answer helps immensely. As winemaking is itself a flow from one activity to another, it makes sense that answers cover the winemaking process in a coherent way. A solid introduction alluding to the points that will be discussed is important. With winemaking, as the reach is often broad, keeping a focus is essential. Many candidates, even the better ones, tended to overlook the use of oenological tannins in winemaking. Points raised could have been in connection with stabilising the colour with tannin or improving structural elements of early-pressed wines. Candidates must not just focus on the premium end of the market - it could be argued that judicial tannin management is more important at "entry level" - pressing off skins before the end of primary fermentation is common practice. Many candidates tended to focus too much on fermentation and not give a full answer. For those that covered pressing, few really explained with any level of authority the way tannin can be managed in a press through fractions - fining pressing fractions (and free run) is an important way of managing tannin. In relation to the extraction process, candidates should have a clear understanding of the various cap management techniques, how they differ and why they are used. They should have also included some discussion of post fermentation maceration and other post fermentation operations that can manage tannin (ie microoxygenation, ageing in barrels, etc). Lastly, as a caution, be very wary of making derogatory remarks about certain winemaking methods (i.e. rotary fermenters). These comments can show a lack of understanding of the wine industry as a whole and can 'make the Examiners blood heat up!' (to quote one Examiner). 4.

commentary: Discuss the impact of malolactic fermentation, or its absence, on wine style. Key Understanding: This question is looking for the candidate to give a concise definition of what malolactic fermentation is and does, and then apply this to a number of wine styles outlining the relevant impact that MLF has on that style. It is important to give examples across styles from sparkling, white, red and possibly fortified to substantiate the argument. Candidates must demonstrate a thorough understanding of the MLF process - bacteria involved, fermentation temperature, possible risks - and discuss this in relation to the impact on wine style (acid reduction, bi-products of the MLF). 11 Perhaps because this question seemed fairly straightforward at first glance, a great many candidates chose it. Only one really gave an excellent and comprehensive answer along with a few passable ones. The rest seemed to struggle. The main cause of concern was a failure to define clearly the bacteria responsible for malolactic fermentation. Students need to update their knowledge of LAB strains. To start with, Oenococcus oeni has the greatest capacity to grow in an acidic environment and in the presence of 10% ethanol. It was previously called Leuconostoc oenos but the name was changed in the late 1990's and therefore scripts should be clear in referencing the current name. Oenococcus oeni is the most common species to conduct the MLF but other bacterial populations can be found and are generally considered to be spoilage bacteria. In addition several students seem convinced that Oenococcus oeni doesn't occur naturally - perhaps due to the fact that winemakers do add it as a cultured bacterium. With this in mind, students were likely to run into trouble later in the paper if their introduction wasn't watertight. It also required careful planning - this question required more than the winemaking flow-chart approach which can be used on so many Paper 2 answers. The best looked to break it down into red wines, white wines/sparkling bases and other impacts such as microbiological. Too many candidates simply dismissed the impact of MLF on red wine as 'all red wines go through MLF'. Clearly, there were more marks to be gained in considering the impacts on white and sparkling wines but the impact of MLF on red wines as well as reds that don't go through MLF could have had a paragraph of discussion. Apart from Nouveau styles, there are a number of sweet red wines on the market now that do not undergo MLF. More importantly a number of candidates attempted the question centred almost exclusively on the impact of MLF on Chardonnay with a brief mention of aromatic white wines and thus didn't answer the question with sufficient breadth. The main issue however seemed to be technical misunderstandings. Not only were the bacteria involved a confusion for candidates but also the basic science of MLF. pH levels were all over the place and either rose or fell after MLF. Ideal temperatures to conduct MLF also varied from ''low 12ºC'' to "high 36ºC". 5.

commentary: What are the winemaker's options and challenges in colour management for different wine styles? Key Understanding: - A broad essay inviting the candidate to demonstrate their knowledge of a wide variety of process options and the core relationship between colour and skins. The inter-related notions of tannin management and also pH and wine stability are critical. Spoilage factors from rot- related colour destabilization through to oxidation - deliberate or accidental - post fermentation should also have been addressed. Despite being a large topic area with many different areas to address, this should have been a relatively straightforward question to approach. As with all large, open questions where there is the temptation to write too much, a good, clear introduction is necessary. A well-structured introduction lays out the map for answering the question - candidates who have one generally stand a good chance of passing. Paper 2 answers generally benefit from using the natural structure and 12 chronology of the winemaking process as a basis for their structure - for the Examiner it is logical and easy to follow and shows an organised pattern of thinking. It also helps the candidate identify areas of interest that might easily be forgotten under the pressure of the Exam. Most candidates seemed comfortable covering colour extraction techniques in different winemaking styles, but a number of candidates simply described the practices in obtaining colour, answering the first part of the question only. Others used statements like "high temperatures" and "longer time" - more specific, factual insight was required. Candidates also often failed to mention, or showed poor understanding of, winemaking processes post-fermentation, additions (tannin, colour, enzymes, oak) and fining, as well as the role of oxygen. The best answers covered at least a few of these areas, giving a much more complete answer to the question. With such large questions it's critical to have a light touch with each area of the answer, not to get bogged down in overly detailed description of what one particular winemaker does as an example. Passing answers normally have a good tempo and a logical flow - and the Examiner should of course never be questioning a candidate's technical knowledge or assumptions about winemaking practices. 6.

commentary: Examine the pros and cons of skin contact during the winemaking process. Key Understanding: Although the question seems straightforward, it is very important to clarify how it will be approached. Candidates must provide a useful definition of skin contact and should make it clear that this relates to red, white and rosé wines and can be applied to all wine styles (table, sparkling and fortified). Candidates should demonstrate a good understanding of the processes involved with each wine colour and style and use examples from around the world to support their statements. The question can thus be approached either through each category of wine or by the various outcomes that will be affected by skin contact. A similar style question to the previous one, answered perhaps slightly better with a handful of good passes. Also quite similar to a question from last year's Exam so perhaps candidates were well prepared for this very topical area. As per the previous question, failure often resulted because of poor structure or incomplete answers that failed to address major winemaking styles (red, rosé, white etc). While it can be useful to clearly state the areas you will address in your answer it is not acceptable to state that you will omit areas like red winemaking because all red wines have skin contact. There is definitely a trend for candidates to list all they know about a topic area as a form of answer - this will rarely pass, or producing a load of examples with no context or argument linking them. Time and again the one thing that appears lacking is evidence of original thinking, or critical analysis. Few candidates are able to present examples in a way that shows there are different ways to the same solution (e.g. winemaker 1 does A to arrive at C, while winemaker 2 does B to arrive at C) or that one can use the same techniques to arrive at different outcomes (e.g. winemaker 1 punches down because they like gentle tannin extraction, while winemaker 2 punches down to achieve full extraction). In this way the candidate can demonstrate that the world of wine is complex and subjective, highly localised and global, and ever changing - and that they understand it. 13 A number of introductions end with sentences like, 'This essay will examine…' and then repeat the question, failing to refer the Examiner to what the candidate intends to write and conveys a lack of mastery or flow on the topic. Good, passing answers are detailed but do not waste words or repeat them. Good (but all too few) answers to this question broached summary concepts, for instance that all wines experience an element of skin contact, or that there has been a trend in the past 10 years to aim for more extraction on whites and less extraction on reds. Such answers showed understanding as well as knowledge, covering a range of skin contact methods and their risks. 14

Your answer may consider the whole grape growing and winemaking process. A very varied standard of answers with marks ranging from 20s to high 70s. This showed that the question could be answered well. However far too many candidates seemed unaware of the difference between bacteria and fungi (different kingdoms of life!) and wasted time talking about Brettanomyces and yeast. A definition of "spoilage" would have been useful here as too many talked about general microbial issues in the vineyards and wasted time rather than focusing on the negative effect on the wine itself. Acetobacter and LAB were the main issues to be covered here but several candidates failed to mention LAB and thus could not gain good marks if ignoring approximately half the required coverage. Some technical and numerical detail was essential here to gain good marks. 2.

commentary: What should a winemaker's main considerations be when preparing a finished wine for bottling? This question provided the highest pass rate on this paper, perhaps because it could be answered well by covering practical aspects and using examples rather than having to show high levels of technical understanding. This was quite a broad question so it was important that candidate did show adequate breadth of knowledge. Many candidates simply failed to cover enough ground - the answer needed to cover 15 wine stability but also legal conformity and chemical analysis, and many answers only did part of this. question_text: Who is making money in the wine industry and why? Discuss in detail three specific examples of profitable wine businesses from different parts of the wine industry supply chain.
paper_preamble: 2016 MW Theory Exam Paper Four - Examiners' Report Simon Thorpe MW General comments Despite a good overall pass rate of approximately 30%, this year we saw an increased number of candidates who were competent at producing a technically sound set of answers for this paper, but who lacked a sufficient depth of knowledge and insight to demonstrate the required level to become an MW. paper_preamble: 2016 MW Theory Exam Paper Five - Examiners' Report Beverley Blanning MW General comments Paper 5 is, perhaps more than any other paper, a test of written communication skills. These results demonstrate that a good number of candidates in this year's theory exam came into the exam room with an appropriate level of knowledge and understanding and, importantly, knew how to deploy that knowledge to good effect in response to the questions set. Candidates would be well advised to gauge the level of depth and detail required for a successful response to a question at MW level. Many of the questions set could have been answered in a superficial manner with a basic level of detail, but the MW exam does require a certain precision and insight, of which candidates should be very conscious. In combination with an appropriate level of depth and detail, examiners are also looking for evidence of analytical thought. Very often, simply repeating processes or procedures will not suffice. Equally an overabundance of examples can sometimes mask a lack of fundamental understanding. Examiners across all theory papers this year commented on the repeated use of a limited number of examples. On theory paper 2, one examiner noted 21 out of 56 papers using the same reference to Domaine Dujac. While it is not unsurprising that material from seminars may be widely cited, it does not indicate a broad frame of reference. While the more commonly used examples may for very good reasons be seen as "go to" examples, examples taken from a candidate's own experience and enquiry, used appropriately, will stand out all the more. However, a word of caution; when using examples over-familiarity, even if those individuals being cited are well-known to the candidate, does not strike a suitable tone: "At Churton in Marlborough, Sam will decide to include stems…", and in another example: "According to Mike, the perceived benefit of inclusion of stems…". It should be emphasised that those candidates whose first language is not English, and who are not extremely comfortable writing in English, should seriously consider writing in their native language. In summary, candidates looking to elevate their marks would be well advised to consider first whether they are writing with an appropriate level of depth and detail, secondly whether they are showing evidence of critical analysis. commentary: Old vines have a mystique to them. What are the practical challenges and solutions to maintaining vineyards of old vines? The topic of this question is one which fascinates anyone interested in wine, everyone has an opinion about the superiority of old vine wine! But this question was all about the unique viticultural challenges old vines present in order to continue their existence. It was important to define old vines; Examiners saw everything from 15 to 20 years old as a minimum age, to 60 years. Considering that the average lifespan today globally for vines is in the 20 to 30 year range, a passing paper had to consider old vines in the context of the location being 12 discussed, and be clear about how this definition is often conditioned by regulations (e.g. the Barossa Charter), the historical nature of a vineyard region, or its modernity. Provided examples were given which accorded with the writer's premise, different definitions for old vines were allowed. This question required a substantial knowledge about what problems confront older vines; whether these are related to poor vigour, decrease in productivity, susceptibility to disease, especially trunk diseases or pruning wounds. Not addressing these issues and focussing mainly on the potentially higher quality from a subjective belief in old vines making the best wines, without the critical examination dictated by the question, resulted in failure. The issue of 'maintenance' had to be addressed. The economics of maintaining an old vineyard had also to be considered, particularly in light of increasing mechanization in vineyards with lower costs, vs. the expensive manual labour that old vines almost always require. As the Examiners noted repeatedly the opposite is true, as evidenced by their longevity under diverse, often harsh conditions, in places like South Africa, Australia, Santorini and elsewhere. A key challenge for maintaining old vineyards is the difficulty/inability to use more mechanization for their care. This was certainly something that a passing paper had to address; a number of papers did not do so, or only with a minor reference. Older vines require more personal, experienced care, which is difficult to mechanise, though not impossible given enough money and knowledge of a vineyard's capacity for a radical change in its make-up. Many of the unsuccessful candidates, whilst perhaps having the necessary knowledge, were unable to use it effectively. Candidates would be well advised to gauge the level of depth and detail required for a successful response to a question at MW level. Many of the questions set could have been answered in a superficial manner with a basic level of detail, but the MW exam does require a certain precision and insight, of which candidates should be very conscious. In combination with an appropriate level of depth and detail, examiners are also looking for evidence of analytical thought. Very often, simply repeating processes or procedures will not suffice. Equally an overabundance of examples can sometimes mask a lack of fundamental understanding. Examiners across all theory papers this year commented on the repeated use of a limited number of examples. On theory paper 2, one examiner noted 21 out of 56 papers using the same reference to Domaine Dujac. While it is not unsurprising that material from seminars may be widely cited, it does not indicate a broad frame of reference. commentary: Which winemaking decisions affect the ageing potential of a finished wine? This was another popular question which was focussed on the processes and choices made during winemaking and post-fermentation maturation. The candidate needed to provide a sensible definition of the scope of winemaking - some limited consideration of the vineyard processes was allowed but the primary focus should have been on the vinification process. Ageing potential needed to be defined, finished wine needed to be defined. Examples, as always, needed to be supportive of arguments. One examiner asked: "How do some candidates think a list of examples is enough to pass?" Students should have discussed why a particular process affects the ageing potential of a wine. As always, still wine, sparkling and fortified wine should have been discussed, as well as entry level through to ultra-premium wines. Too many candidates focussed solely on the premium end of the market and neglected entry level wines. Interestingly, too many candidates only discussed red wines. There should have been plenty of scope for candidates to provide meaningful examples of what certain winemakers choose to do, why, and the impact on ageing potential. Lack of essay structure, no definition, limited scope and failure to discuss the "whys and wherefores" were the most common errors. commentary: How does a laboratory analysis of a wine help the quality control manager make decisions at bottling? Bottling is a key step in ensuring this and is the last opportunity to make adjustments. Lab analysis is a tool that provides relevant technical information to allow appropriate decisions about treatments and handling (candidates should show an understanding of what these might be - to cover final filtration, additives, microbial stability, hazes, why and what action might be taken). A number of candidates lacked focus or simply missed too many key issues. Candidates needed to consider both quality checks on wine and checks on the packaging process and dry goods, as well as 17 compliance with product specification. Too many candidates simply described the bottling process and failed to consider the quality control part of the question and showed lack of awareness of key QC analyses for wine and why they are carried out. Consideration of HACCP and critical control points is always useful in a question that mentions bottling. Quality control is part of the overall quality assurance process, and wine is a foodstuff which must comply with legislative and regulatory standards (so an awareness of EU legislation and ISO requirements is helpful). A lot of candidates missed the critical "why" part which is implied in the question, and without considering this, their answers were too superficial and lacked any analytical depth. The safety of staff handling the liquid and the packaging is also critical (with risks such as broken glass, noise, heavy lifting and exposure to health risks). Many candidates stumbled at this first hurdle: either they failed to define the term, or their essays showed that they had not grasped the meaning of the question. This led to simplistic answers with the inevitable conclusion that wine is 'a good thing', which is not what we were asking. It is always advisable to consider both sides of the question, in other words, the arguments for and against. Arguments that might support the idea of wine being a social good might include: its cultural, religious and historical importance; it supports small agricultural economies; it facilitates social cohesion and well-being; it generates tax income; it has certain associations with longevity and good health. Arguments against could include: social and health problems; religious objections; legislation and taxation; costs to society. Many answers were superficial, limited in scope, one-sided and lacking in examples. There was a lot of content about responsible drinking, which is not really relevant to this question. The examiners noted that some candidates persist in giving wine special status within the alcohol sector, implying that wine drinkers are never binge drinkers nor alcoholics. Such a line of argument would require strong supporting evidence to be taken seriously. This was a question that invited examination of the many contentious issues surrounding wine. It was remarkable that, while the answer to the question would undoubtedly be a firm 'no' from many (if not most) in society, hardly any candidates considered this possibility, with 21 of the 24 answers concluding that wine was a social good. 24 Question 2:

commentary: Is elitism an inherent problem in the world of wine? This was not a popular question, but most of those who chose to tackle it did well. Critical to success was understanding the meaning of elitism. This proved problematic for some, who confused elitism with inequality and even sexism. 25 If correctly defined, there were many avenues to be explored to address whether elitism is an inherent problem in wine. An historical perspective was needed, with comparison to present day attitudes. Whether or not elitism is considered an inherent problem requires candidates to examine whether this is a perceived problem somehow related to wine more than other goods, so reference to other markets would have been helpful also. Other areas that could have been addressed include: actual or perceived elitism; wine classification systems; the role of wine qualifications; sales channels and changes in the way wine is bought and sold; whether elitism is a problem, or a positive in some markets or circles; who suffers from elitism and who benefits? 5.

commentary: Do wine consumers need wine experts? This was another popular question. Sadly, it was poorly answered by most candidates. The question needed a really clear and broad definition of 'experts', including media commentators, auctioneers, MWs, buyers, retailers, winemakers, consultants, educators etc, and understanding of the varying and different types of wine expertise. A large number of candidates restricted their definition to journalists and therefore gave very incomplete answers. Most also missed the opportunity to talk about the importance of experts involved in the production of wine, which was a significant omission. Also important was to distinguish between different types of wine consumer, as there will be different requirements of expertise for different types of consumer (generational, geographical, socio-economic, education level, etc). As always, we were looking for a global perspective, and for candidates to demonstrate an understanding of the dynamic nature of how and why consumers might need wine experts. An appreciation of the changing perception of experts and the rise in importance of peer reviews was also an area to explore.
